objects.body: The algorithm will be different, probably. I haven't found anything in the papers, but I have some ideas to explore. If they don't work out there's always the approach from V2 to fall back on, but I think I can do better. (:

So cache quantization is implemented now. It's a variant of the same technique used in V2, but now with separate bitrates (2-8 bpw plus 0.5 bpw of overhead) for K and V channels. Works a little better than in V2, and it's more flexible.

I experimented with realtime trellis quantization, learned channel scales, autoencoders and more, but so far with little success, and not enough benefit to justify the overhead and complexity. There's still much to explore, though. For instance, I think it should be possible to learn an optimal rotation for the keys in a given layer, under a quantization constraint, then bake the same transformation into the Q and K projections, preserving their dot product.

But for the time being, it's too much of a side quest, and I need to focus on some other stuff first. In the meantime you can get very usable results from k4v3 quantization, and more-or-less lossless quantization with k5v4. And it's "usable" down to k3v2, depending on the use case. Might make the model more creative or something, who knows (:. I still have to rig up some tests to see if it holds up over long contexts.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ea2adb25-00f4-4dbb-875f-1150ce2f4039)

(Note that this is a single-sample eval so assume an uncertainty of +/- 3% or so. Still have yet to figure out why Llama 3.1 Instruct models improve on HumanEval with more quantization, up to a point. This happens with weight quantization, too.)

Epic!

Been dragging my heels, but I've already got eval scripts I'm working on.

title: `cogito-v1-preview-qwen-32B` generates incoherent output for bpw <= 2.5

objects.body:
I have quantized [deepcogito/cogito-v1-preview-qwen-32B](https://huggingface.co/deepcogito/cogito-v1-preview-qwen-32B) for tests, and found that the following bpw worked perfectly, with no noticeable performance degradation:

* 3.0bpw
* 4.0bpw
* 5.0bpw
* 6.0bpw
* 8.0bpw

However, the following bpw are completely incoherent:

* 2.0bpw
* 2.25bpw
* 2.5bpw

They output random non-latin characters for every input I have tried.

I have uploaded these models here: https://huggingface.co/oobabooga/cogito-v1-preview-qwen-32B-exl3

objects.body:
So I've spent the past couple of days investigating this, and I'm no closer to a real answer. There's something very strange about a few specific tensors in the model and they just don't want to quantize correctly below 3 bpw with the normal regularization scheme. It also seems to affect QwQ-32B.

I'll figure it out eventually, but in the meantime I've added a workaround that tries to detect when the full regularization is actually needed and disables the output channel normalization otherwise, which seems to have done the trick, and I'm able to quantize it at 2 bpw. Sadly it does mean the broken versions need to be converted again.

Thanks for looking into this. Having to reconvert some broken or sub-optimal quants is entirely expected with EXL3 at such an early stage.

I don't know if it helps at all, but I put this issue in a long conversation I had with Claude a few days ago (where I was trying to understand how EXL3 works by looking at its source code), and the model brought up

```python
    diag = H_diag.sqrt()  # Square root of diagonal elements of Hessian
    cv = diag.std() / diag.mean()  # Coefficient of variation
    apply_out_scales = cv < threshold  # e.g., threshold = 1.0
```

as a possible alternative to

```python
    diag = H_diag.sqrt()
    diag, _ = torch.sort(diag, descending = True)
    cutoff = diag.shape[0] // 50
    skew_factor = diag[:cutoff].sum() / diag.sum()
    if verbose:
        print(f"     - input state skew: {skew_factor.item():.6f}")
    
    if force_out_scales is None:
        apply_out_scales = skew_factor.item() < 0.15
    else:
        apply_out_scales = force_out_scales
```

using the "coefficient of variation (CV) of the Hessian diagonal".

Of course I have no idea what any of this means, if this improves anything, if there is a more fundamental way to tackle this, but this has 1 parameter istead of 2 so I figured I should share it to see if it gives you any idea.
I have confirmed that the quants work well with the latest exllamav3 and have uploaded the fixed quants.
@oobabooga Out of curiosity, how does Cognito 32B perform at the lower quant levels, if you've even tested it enough to make that determination?
I find that for bpw >= 3.0 the quants are very good, below that there is measurable degradation in my small test but the models remain functional all the way to 2.0 bpw

objects.body:
The problem seems to be the tokenizer for the finetuned model. If you look in `tokenizer.json`, at the top of the file someone has added this:

```json
  "truncation": {
    "direction": "Right",
    "max_length": 4096,
    "strategy": "LongestFirst",
    "stride": 0
  },
```

I'm not sure what the purpose of that is, as it prevents the `tokenizers` library from tokenizing more than 4096 tokens, and the EXL3 quantizer needs much more than that. I suspect it's unintentionally left over from the finetuning process. But I'll make a note to check for it since apparently it's a thing that can happen, and the quantizer should notice rather than giving a cryptic CUDA error down the line.

In the meantime, quantization should work if you replace it with:

```json
  "truncation": null,
```

Or alternatively just copy `tokenizer.json` over from Phi-4, since they seem to be identical otherwise.
Okay, turns out you can just override that feature when loading the tokenizer. Problem solved.

objects.title: Any chance of a single model file?

objects.body:
ExLlama uses the HF format, which is how new models are normally released. The only thing changed during quantization are the tensors themselves, meaning everything else can leverage existing libraries for tokenization, instruction templates and more. It's also an open, widely adopted format that other tools can work with, to inspect and modify tensor data, tweak config settings, swap out tokenizer models, etc. And of course it keeps the door open to using EXL3 models in other frameworks like Transformers and vLLM, which in turn only need a way to read and process the quantized weights. And of course you have the option of running models downloaded straight from HF without converting anything. The converter relies on this ability anyway, so it's convenient not needing two separate code paths for quantized and unquantized models, respectively.

All in all it's a lot to give up, and a lot of extra development overhead, for the convenience of having everything packed in a single file as opposed to a single directory.

Fair enough. I run things in a VM and tend to download from a browser so it is a hassle, but the hassle doesn't seem worth the trade offs. Thanks for explaining the reasoning behind the design. You have smarts I wish I had :)

title: Build Failure on Windows: CUDA 12.4 / PyTorch 2.7.0+cu126 / VS 2022

objects.body:
Hi,

I'm encountering compilation errors when trying to build exllamav3 from source on Windows. I've followed the installation instructions and attempted several troubleshooting steps

Environment:

    OS: Windows 11

    Python: 3.11.0

    CUDA Toolkit: 12.4

    PyTorch: 2.7.0+cu126 (Installed via pip install torch==2.7.0+cu126 ... --index-url ...)

    Visual Studio: Community 2022 (with "Desktop development with C++" workload, using latest MSVC v143 toolset - 14.43.34808)

Steps to Reproduce:

    Cloned the repository.

    Ensured CUDA Toolkit 12.4 and VS 2022 (with C++ workload) are installed correctly (where cl works in Developer Prompt).

    Installed PyTorch 2.7.0+cu126 successfully.

    Opened a Developer Command Prompt for VS 2022.

    Navigated to the exllamav3 directory.

    Ran set DISTUTILS_USE_SDK=1.

    Ran pip install -r requirements.txt (after commenting out the torch line to keep the manually installed CUDA version).

    Ran pip install .

Expected Behavior:

The pip install . command should successfully compile the C++/CUDA extensions.

Actual Behavior:

The installation fails during the compilation of the C++/CUDA extensions (Building wheel for exllamav3 (setup.py) ... error). Key errors observed in the build log include:

      
# Errors during C++ compilation (.cpp files):
C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python311\Lib\site-packages\torch\include\c10/util/safe_numerics.h(23): error C3861: '_addcarry_u64': identifier not found

# Errors during CUDA compilation (.cu files):
C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v12.4\include\cuda_fp16.hpp(1890): error: asm operand type size(8) does not match type/size implied by constraint 'r'
C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v12.4\include\cuda_bf16.hpp(1868): error: asm operand type size(8) does not match type/size implied by constraint 'r'
C:/Users/user/AppData/Local/Programs/Python/Python311/Lib\site-packages/torch/include\c10/core/TensorImpl.h(3166): error: static assertion failed with "Actual and Expected sizes of a field did not match!"

# Final error message:
subprocess.CalledProcessError: Command '['ninja', '-v']' returned non-zero exit status 1.
...
RuntimeError: Error compiling objects for extension

(Full logs can be provided if needed)

Troubleshooting Steps Taken:

    Verified VS 2022 Build Tools installation (Repair, checked workloads/components).

    Verified cl.exe is found in the Developer Command Prompt path.

    Ensured correct CUDA_HOME and CUDA_PATH environment variables are set.

    Modified setup.py to remove hardcoded "C:/cuda" paths and use CUDA_HOME environment variable instead.

    Tried installing with EXLLAMA_NOCOMPILE=1 (JIT mode). The installation command succeeded, but the import failed at runtime with the same compilation errors shown above.

    Tried PyTorch 2.5.1+cu121 (conflicts with requirements.txt torch>=2.6.0).

    Tried older MSVC v14.38 toolset (did not resolve these specific compilation errors).

Question:

Is this combination of CUDA 12.4 / PyTorch 2.7.0+cu126 / latest VS 2022 known to be incompatible with the current exllamav3 source? Is there a recommended, specific set of toolchain versions known to work for building on Windows?

objects.body:
FlashInfer is too problematic at the moment anyway. Some unsupported head dimensions, packaging is difficult because there are too many kernel variants (needs either a custom build for EXL3 or relying on users having build prerequisites installed to use their JIT system), and it would need some support functions to be functionally equivalent to Flash Attention (how the paged cache is managed, etc.).

title: VRAM+RAM support

objects.body:
I wonder if for ExllamaV3 partial or full RAM offloading would be a possibility or if it will be strictly GPU only? I ask because Readme mentions Deepseek support in the works, but most people run R1 or V3 on combination of RAM and VRAM (including me), or even with RAM only.

It would be so cool if it would be possible to use both RAM and VRAM, not just for Deepseek but could be useful for example for smaller models, for example 4-5bpw quants of upcoming Qwen3-30B-A3B could run with just 8GB-12GB cards and exl3 more efficient quants could provide either better quality at the same size or allow to fit more layers on GPU. So if such feature is possible, I believe it would be useful to many people who are short on VRAM but still want to run a model that does not fully fit into it.

Please feel free to close this if it is not planned or cannot be implemented.
objects.title: VRAM+RAM support

objects.body:
Not the dev, but at risk of sounding blunt, it would be easier to add exllama-like features to llama.cpp, which was set up for CPU/hybrid inference from the get-go, or other CPU-focused engines like Intel's.

If you wish to run Deepseek, ik_llama.cpp is what you want, which has implented MLA attention, different quantization than base llama.cpp, and is optimized *explicitly* for hybrid inference of big MoEs like deepseek: https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/

I bet the new Qwen MoEs will be a major focus, too. And its quantization is not quite as space-efficent as exl3, but its very fast on CPU.

objects.body:
Yes, ik_llama.cpp is excellent and the only one that actually works well for VRAM+RAM inference at the moment, based on my experience (ktransformers I could not even built and I think they lack easy to use multi-gpu support, and also ktransformers focus more on Intel than AMD CPUs).

Anyway, I thought it is still worth asking if it is potentially possible or planned for ExllamaV3... since exl3 quants I think are more efficient than GGUF ones, and therefore could potentially either provide higher quality for the same memory or fit to a smaller system. And with MoE models becoming more common while high VRAM GPUs still remain very expensive, demand for VRAM+RAM inference  probably will be higher than before. But like I said, if it is out of scope for ExllamaV3 please feel to close...

It is hard for me to guess how CPU efficient exl3 could be, but I can tell that GGUF is not exactly CPU efficient either, in fact I hit CPU bottleneck with 64 cores before I hit 8 channel DDR4 memory bandwidth bottleneck when running Deepseek full model.

objects.body:
Would be awesome, but this might open a can of worms down the line.

There is support for VRAM-ram offload in the nvidia driver (Shared memory) on windows, but last time i checked its kind of jank and doesnt work on linux. There are some other ways tapping into ram with cuda operations im not really aware any projects using it(vLLM maybe?). However this defeats the purpose of the whole exllama library of fast inference, so as @Downtown-Case said you have better luck just using llama.cpp.

Vram paging in Windows is aimed more at gaming, when the app allocates and loads a few things into memory it *perhaps shouldn't*, and doesn't strictly need at the moment. You may get a big hitch when the game needs the texture (or whatever was paged out), but then the game runs normally.

It is *not* useful for LLM running; it's faster to just do the memory management yourself (which would still be quite slow).

vLLM will swap in/out of CPU memory for caching purposes, but (AFAIK) not for the "core" model loop.

Theoretically, CXL will faciliatate *operating* out of CPU memory, but we are not there yet unless you own an AMD MI300. Theoretically, hybrid inference with your IGP might do better, but there are many software barriers to that.

Trying to do GPU work out of CPU memory is a hard problem, and current ML solutions tend to work best just doing some work on the CPU and building the framework around that. Exllama's approach is more "compress everything compute-heavy so it fits on GPUs," taking advantage of gpu-centric approaches/frameworks to do it... though who knows what the future holds.

objects.body: Yes, optimizing ffn offloading can be surprisingly beneficial, especially focusing on the ffn exps with MoE provides impressive benefits. Having something similar in EXL3 would be a game changer.

Curious: is there still a plan to some day support shared experts (egs.., Kimi K2, Deepseeks) in exllama? Not necessarily with CPU offloading, just supporting them period. Are shared experts the only issue with those model architectures or is there some other complication? Is it just an issue of prioritizing, or some other bottleneck like not having enough hardware to test?

Shared experts are already supported. What's missing are routing groups and MLA (latent attention). The former may not be strictly needed and isn't too hard to incorporate anyway, but MLA requires swapping out the attn backend which in turn affects the generator and paged caching mechanisms. So it's a big rewrite for models that very few people have the hardware to run and I can't even test myself.
When it comes to MLA, there's already a successor in DSA as well now, isn't there? But to what degree that will be adopted in models more people can run is another matter.

I think DSA still looks like MLA when it comes to KV cache shapes though, not sure it makes the job any easier for turbo.

> So it's a big rewrite for models that very few people have the hardware to run and I can't even test myself.

I think that's probably the main reason Exllama doesn't support DS/Kimi. Turbo has already revolutionized local running for a lot of big models they themselves probably were never interested in, and models/features that most of the user-base of Exllama likely doesn't care about (like high bit-depth quants of larger models with TP over multi-GPU), so I already think this is an awesome project that goes above-and-beyond what the apparent stated mission is. I believe turbo is aware of this, it was _one_ of the reasons for shifting to Exllamv3 I think. But I can see how they would draw a line somewhere to prioritize.

That said, I think the new Mistral Large 3 is of comparable size to DS, but I don't think it uses MLA/DSA. Maybe that one is more straightforward to support?

There is now optional CPU offloading for MoE layers, and the K/V cache has a second-tier CPU backup. MLA is supported, and DeepseekV3 works as long as there are no top-k routing groups (might add later)

title: Auto-YaRN for Qwen3? Maybe even set it dynamically?

objects.body:
It appears Qwen3 is using YaRN for long contexts, like Qwen 2.5:

> The maximum context length in pre-training for Qwen3 models is 32,768 tokens. It can be extended to 131,072 tokens with RoPE scaling techniques. We have validated the performance with YaRN.

https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3/blob/main/docs/source/inference/transformers.md#enabling-long-context

Editing the config file for the desired context is... less than ideal for users.

*However*, they mention this little nugget:

> Transformers implements static YaRN, which means the scaling factor remains constant regardless of input length, potentially impacting performance on shorter texts. We advise adding the rope_scaling configuration only when processing long contexts is required. It is also recommended to modify the factor as needed. For example, if the typical context length for your application is 65,536 tokens, it would be better to set factor as 2.0

The default factor is 4.0, and currently the exllama code will stick to that if the 'default' long context configuration is present: https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/blob/0ff9fd2e39f6307e54358fd1a48a50b5cf7307f8/exllamav3/util/rope.py#L130-L159

But it *appears* a more optimal thing to do is ignore the rope_scaling factor, and statically set it with `(context length of the loaded model)/original_max_position_embeddings`, which would be 2.0 for 64K, 3.0 for 96K, and so on.

This is trivially easy to implement, but the question is if exllamav3 should set it automatically like that. *I say* it should, as most users aren't going to dig into how YaRN scaling works and match the scaling factor to their specified context length. 

***

...But what would be *even more optimal* would be to dynamically set the scaling factor per request. For instance, if a 64K request was recieved, set it to 2.0. A 96K one, 3.0. So each request gets the optimal factor.

Even better would be to disable YaRN entirely for requests under 32K.

...Is this practical to do? I seem to remember it not being practical in exllamav2.

objects.body:
The RoPE parameters has an override that could be used at load time, though it's currently only used for longrope:

```py
@dataclass
class RopeSettings:
    head_dim: int = 128
    rope_theta: float = 10000.0
    rope_scaling: dict | None = None
    partial_rotary_factor: float = 1.0
    max_position_embeddings: int | None = None
    original_max_position_embeddings: int | None = None
    rope_style: RopeStyle = RopeStyle.NEOX
    override_max_position_embeddings: int | None = None
```

It's a total nightmare to deal with, though, honestly. Changing the scaling factor dynamically breaks just about every assumption made in the generator, and I'm not sure how to even approach stuff like a new set of frequencies per request, since the generator can batch together sequences of different length. It can also reuse cached values from a previous sequence, and that would have to go as well if position IDs have to be reinterpreted based on the overall max sequence length.

Ah, yeah, it's *not* worth breaking anything. Forget per-request dynamism. It doesn't seem that great past 32K it in my few API tests anyway.

How about a log warning? Maybe a print statement along the lines of "WARNING: A scaling factor of 2.0 is recommended for a context size of 65536!"

An interesting datapoint: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-32B/discussions/18

TL;DR: Qwen3 32B 3.45bpw, squeezed into 24GB, got a math/reasoning question from a 107K prompt! Exllamav2/Qwen2.5 (with YaRN) wasn't even close to that in my testing, though admittedly I never tested QwQ like that.

In other words, YaRN is surprisingly effective with Qwen3, and setting the correct scaling factor seems to be important.

This is odd. Do other models have this issue, or is it just GLM4-9B?

If I try it here it seems to work:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e124c1ad-13aa-45bc-afdc-0fc470943915)

It messes up at the end, likely because it's instruct tuned and supposed to be used with the correct template. If I use GLM mode it seems less flaky:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fa593cd2-583f-474d-8a83-d50fa1d51c52)

This is the 4bpw model from the link you provided. It's very possible there's an issue with inference on Windows. But it would help to know if it's just this model or inference is breaking in general.

Another thing that could help would be, if you have enough VRAM (24 GB should do), to try running `chat.py` with the unquantized model.

I haven't gotten to testing any of the Command-A models yet, getting stuck on some poorly conditioned tensors in Command-R-Plus that refuse to quantize correctly due to extreme outliers and what looks like a crude lobotomy:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e804c4f0-6bb9-41b7-be23-754ba0f6682f)

So I don't know if Command-A inherited those issues, and (especially since this is a finetuned variant) you should definitely pay close attention to the error on the early layers. It could save me some time if you have the console output from the first layers as well (not necessarily in verbose mode.)

That said, this error looks like a simple overflow following the activation function in one particular layer (by the looks of it, in a single channel?), which might be solved by clamping the activations. I will have to spend a little time investigating. :|

objects.body: I've reimplemented retrying_cholesky from https://www.tensorflow.org/probability/api_docs/python/tfp/experimental/distributions/marginal_fns/retrying_cholesky and clamped the activations in https://github.com/memmaptensor/exllamav3/commit/32acf60abb73c64cf20de43b7ecbceea2c840d30. This was also an issue on some Llama3.1 finetunes with ill-conditioned tensors. Haven't tried the quantized models yet, but the quantization seems to be going fine for now.

There were some GEMM errors at the end of quantization from einsum. Replacing it with a chunked impl seemed to work. Command-A appears to be at least coherent on 16k context at 3.32bpw. https://github.com/memmaptensor/exllamav3/commit/fa6b849cb49e5d820161f80d295ad9c1a0b15707

title: Will exl3 quants need requanting later?

objects.body:
Basically, title. If I devote time and energy into quanting exl3, will they have to be re-quanted in a couple months?

Or is exl3 a stable format?

I'm aware a lot of features are a WIP and stuff, so just making sure.
objects.title: Will exl3 quants need requanting later?

objects.body: As a followup question, your github says ampere support is lacking. Is quanting on a 3090 okay, or will there be problems?

I don't intend to make changes to the storage format. If I do, the implementation will retain backwards compatibility with existing quantized models. I wouldn't expect major improvements that would make you want to revisit old models. If there's anything like that it'll be because some new model needs it.

Ampere support isn't lacking in the sense that it doesn't work. Ampere works fine, it's just not at the performance I want it at, yet. Quantization will be somewhat slower on Ampere as well, but this was the case with EXL2 as well. The 4090 is overall a much faster GPU than the 3090, and the only really comparable stat between them is memory size and bandwidth. It just so happens that LLM inference at low batch sizes and for "simple" formats like INT4 is bandwidth limited. I may reach that limit with the EXL3 GEMM kernel at some point, but quantization is not in any way memory bound, so it will always just run faster with more CUDA cores.

objects.body:
Seems like it was due to a mismatch with the conda environment and the compiler from the system, creating a new environment and then:

`conda install -y cmake gxx`

before installing pip install requirements / . fixed the issue. Might be useful in the documentation as I'd expect others to be using fresh conda environments as well. Can't wait for tabbyAPI to support exl3, thanks for all the hard work on exllamav3!

A model explained it as: The __cxa_call_terminate symbol comes from C++ runtime internals. Mixing system compilers with Conda Python will almost always break anything involving native extensions. Stick to a single toolchain — preferably the Conda one — or use system Python + venv, but not both.

Interestingly, I've never had this issue w/ exllamav2, but, since I have the solution above, I'm not really looking into it in depth.

This seems okay, though it should definitely be done with some care. For MLP layers the down projection can be trivially padded with zeros before quantizing, since the extra input channels will never contribute anything to the output. But attention (and down the line convolutions and other stuff) might break in subtle and confusing ways if both input and output channels are padded automatically.

I'll give this a closer look tomorrow. Looks like a very interesting model, too.

By the way, right now it will still error on simultaneous padding.

```py
import torch


def test(in_features, out_features, pad_to):
    w = torch.zeros((out_features, in_features))

    in_features_unpadded = in_features
    in_features = (in_features + pad_to - 1) // pad_to * pad_to
    out_features_unpadded = out_features
    out_features = (out_features + pad_to - 1) // pad_to * pad_to

    padded = torch.zeros((out_features, in_features))
    if out_features != out_features_unpadded:
        padded[: w.shape[0], :] = w
    elif in_features != in_features_unpadded:
        padded[:, : w.shape[1]] = w

    print(w.shape)
    print(padded.shape)


test(64, 128, 8)  # ok
test(64 + 4, 128, 8)  # ok
test(64, 128 + 4, 8)  # ok
test(64 + 4, 128 + 4, 8)  # error
```

import json
import time

import os

import argparse
import threading
import torch
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from socketserver import ThreadingMixIn
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional, Tuple, Union
from queue import Queue
from threading import Lock

# 配置日志
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# 添加项目根目录到路径
script_path = os.path.abspath(__file__)
project_root = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(script_path))
sys.path.insert(0, project_root)

try:
    from exllamav3 import model_init
    from exllamav3.models.model import Model
    from exllamav3.cache.cache import Cache
    from exllamav3.tokenizer.tokenizer import Tokenizer
    from exllamav3.generator.generator import Generator
    from exllamav3.generator.sampler import ComboSampler
    from exllamav3.generator.job import Job
    # 导入聊天模板
    from chat_templates import prompt_formats
except ImportError as e:
    logger.error(f"错误: 未找到所需库。{e}")
    logger.error("请确保已安装PyTorch并且exllamav3库可访问。")
    sys.exit(1)

# 全局变量
model = None
tokenizer = None
generator = None
cache = None
model_name = "exllamav3_model"
prompt_format = None
add_bos = None
system_prompt = None

# 添加请求处理锁
model_lock = Lock()

def initialize_model(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    """初始化模型和相关组件"""
    global model, tokenizer, generator, model_name, cache
    global prompt_format, add_bos, system_prompt

    logger.info(f"初始化模型: {args.model_dir}")
    model, config, cache, tokenizer = model_init.init(args, quiet=True)

    # 设置提示格式
    user_name = args.user_name
    bot_name = args.bot_name
    prompt_format = prompt_formats[args.mode](user_name, bot_name)
    system_prompt = prompt_format.default_system_prompt() if not args.system_prompt else args.system_prompt
    add_bos = prompt_format.add_bos()

    logger.info(f"提示格式设置为: {args.mode}")
    logger.info(f"系统提示: {system_prompt[:50]}..." if len(system_prompt) > 50 else system_prompt)

    if model and cache and tokenizer:
        generator = Generator(model, cache, tokenizer)
        logger.info("Generator已创建")
    else:
        logger.error("由于缺少model、cache或tokenizer，无法初始化generator")
        sys.exit(1)

    # 使用目录名作为默认模型标识符
    model_name = os.path.basename(os.path.normpath(args.model_dir))
    logger.info("初始化完成")

def format_input(messages: List[Dict[str, str]]) -> List[Tuple[str, Optional[str]]]:
    """将API请求中的消息格式化为prompt_format预期的格式"""
    global system_prompt
    
    context = []
    
    for message in messages:
        role = message.get('role', '')
        content = message.get('content', '')
        
        if role == "system":
            # 使用第一个系统消息作为系统提示
            system_prompt = content
        elif role == "user":
            # 添加用户消息到上下文
            context.append((content, None))
        elif role == "assistant":
            # 如果没有前面的用户消息，添加一个占位符
            if len(context) == 0 or context[-1][1] is not None:
                context.append(("", content))
            else:
                # 更新最后一个用户消息，添加助手回复
                user_msg, _ = context[-1]
                context[-1] = (user_msg, content)
    
    return context

def format_chat_prompt(messages: List[Dict[str, str]]) -> str:
    """使用配置的prompt_format将消息列表格式化为提示字符串"""
    global tokenizer, prompt_format, system_prompt
    
    if prompt_format:
        context = format_input(messages)
        return prompt_format.format(system_prompt, context)
    else:
        # 如果prompt_format未设置的备用方案
        prompt = ""
        for msg in messages:
            prompt += f"{msg.get('role', 'unknown')}: {msg.get('content', '')}\n"
        prompt += "assistant:"
        return prompt

class APIHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def _send_response(self, status_code: int, content_type: str, body: str) -> None:
        """发送HTTP响应"""
        self.send_response(status_code)
        self.send_header('Content-Type', content_type)
        self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body.encode('utf-8'))

    def _send_json_response(self, status_code: int, data: Dict[str, Any]) -> None:
        """发送JSON响应"""
        self._send_response(status_code, 'application/json', json.dumps(data))

    def _send_error(self, status_code: int, message: str) -> None:
        """发送错误响应"""
        error_data = {"error": {"message": message, "type": "api_error", "code": None}}
        self._send_json_response(status_code, error_data)

    def _send_sse_chunk(self, data: Union[Dict[str, Any], str]) -> bool:
        """发送Server-Sent Event数据块"""
        try:
            if isinstance(data, str):  # 处理"[DONE]"字符串
                self.wfile.write(f"data: {data}\n\n".encode('utf-8'))
            else:
                self.wfile.write(f"data: {json.dumps(data)}\n\n".encode('utf-8'))
            self.wfile.flush()  # 确保数据立即发送
            return True
        except BrokenPipeError:
            return False  # 如果客户端断开连接则停止流式传输

    def do_OPTIONS(self) -> None:
        """处理OPTIONS请求（CORS预检）"""
        self.send_response(204)
        self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')
        self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Methods', 'POST, GET, OPTIONS')
        self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Headers', 'Content-Type, Authorization')
        self.end_headers()

    def do_GET(self) -> None:
        """处理GET请求"""
        global model, tokenizer, generator, model_name

        if self.path == '/v1/models':
            if not model or not tokenizer or not generator:
                self._send_error(503, "模型尚未初始化")
                return
                
            # 提供基本模型信息
            model_info = {
                "object": "list",
                "data": [{
                    "id": model_name,
                    "object": "model",
                    "created": int(time.time()),
                    "owned_by": "user",
                    "permission": [],
                    "root": model_name,
                    "parent": None,
                }]
            }
            self._send_json_response(200, model_info)
        else:
            self._send_response(200, 'text/plain', 'ExLlamaV3 API服务运行中。使用POST /v1/chat/completions接口。')

    def do_POST(self) -> None:

        global model, tokenizer, generator, model_name, cache, prompt_format, model_lock

        if self.path == '/v1/chat/completions':

            with model_lock:

                    content_length_header = self.headers['Content-Length']
                    if content_length_header is None:
                        self._send_error(411, "需要Content-Length头")
                        return
                        
                    content_length = int(content_length_header)
                    post_data = self.rfile.read(content_length)
                    request_data = json.loads(post_data.decode('utf-8'))
                except (TypeError, ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
                    self._send_error(400, f"无效的JSON请求: {e}")
                    return
                except Exception as e:
                    self._send_error(400, f"读取请求时出错: {e}")
                    return

                # 检查模型是否初始化
                if not model or not tokenizer or not generator or not cache:
                    self._send_error(503, "模型尚未初始化")
                    return

                # 验证消息
                messages = request_data.get('messages')
                if not messages or not isinstance(messages, list):
                    self._send_error(400, "'messages'字段是必需的，且必须是一个列表")
                    return

                # 参数设置
                stream = request_data.get('stream', False)
                max_tokens = request_data.get('max_tokens', 50000)
                temperature = request_data.get('temperature', 0.6)
                top_p = request_data.get('top_p', 0.95)
                top_k = request_data.get('top_k', 50)
                rep_penalty = request_data.get('repetition_penalty', 1.0)
                pres_penalty = request_data.get('presence_penalty', 0.0)
                freq_penalty = request_data.get('frequency_penalty', 0.0)
                min_p = request_data.get('min_p', 0.08)
                requested_model_name = request_data.get('model', model_name)

                # 准备提示
                try:
                    prompt = format_chat_prompt(messages)
                    # 编码提示以获取输入ID
                    input_ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt, add_bos=add_bos, encode_special_tokens=True)
                    prompt_token_count = input_ids.shape[-1]
                except Exception as e:
                    self._send_error(500, f"处理消息或编码提示时出错: {e}")
                    return

                # 检查Token限制
                required_tokens = prompt_token_count + max_tokens
                capacity = cache.max_num_tokens
                if required_tokens > capacity:
                    logger.warning(f"请求被拒绝: 所需token ({required_tokens} = {prompt_token_count}提示 + {max_tokens}最大新token)超过模型容量({capacity})。")
                    error_payload = {
                        "error": {
                            "message": f"请求的token数量({required_tokens})超过模型容量({capacity})。提示token: {prompt_token_count}, 最大新token: {max_tokens}。",
                            "type": "invalid_request_error",
                            "code": "context_length_exceeded"
                        }
                    }
                    self._send_json_response(400, error_payload)
                    return

                # 获取停止条件
                stop_conditions_req = request_data.get('stop', [])
                stop_conditions = []
                if isinstance(stop_conditions_req, list):
                    stop_conditions = stop_conditions_req
                elif isinstance(stop_conditions_req, (str, int)):
                    stop_conditions = [stop_conditions_req]
                
                # 添加prompt_format停止条件
                if prompt_format:
                    format_stop_conditions = prompt_format.stop_conditions(tokenizer)
                    stop_conditions.extend(format_stop_conditions)
                
                # 如果EOS令牌尚未在停止条件中，则添加它
                if tokenizer.eos_token_id is not None and tokenizer.eos_token_id not in stop_conditions:
                    stop_conditions.append(tokenizer.eos_token_id)

                # 设置采样器
                sampler = ComboSampler(
                    rep_p=rep_penalty,
                    pres_p=pres_penalty,
                    freq_p=freq_penalty,
                    rep_sustain_range=1024,
                    rep_decay_range=1024,
                    temperature=temperature,
                    min_p=min_p,
                    top_k=top_k,
                    top_p=top_p,
                    temp_last=True,
                )

                generation_id = f"chatcmpl-{uuid.uuid4()}"
                created_time = int(time.time())

                # 流式响应
                if stream:
                    self.send_response(200)
                    self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/event-stream')
                    self.send_header('Cache-Control', 'no-cache')
                    self.send_header('Connection', 'close')
                    self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')
                    self.end_headers()

                    # 发送初始响应块
                    initial_chunk = {
                        "id": generation_id,
                        "object": "chat.completion.chunk",
                        "created": created_time,
                        "model": requested_model_name,
                        "choices": [{
                            "index": 0,
                            "delta": {"role": "assistant"},
                            "finish_reason": None
                        }]
                    }
                    self._send_sse_chunk(initial_chunk)

                    finish_reason = None
                    job_done = False
                    job = None

                    try:
                        # 创建并入队作业
                        job = Job(
                            input_ids=input_ids,
                            max_new_tokens=max_tokens,
                            sampler=sampler,
                            stop_conditions=stop_conditions,
                        )
                        generator.enqueue(job)

                        # 在作业活动时迭代
                        while generator.num_remaining_jobs() > 0 and not job_done:
                            for r in generator.iterate():
                                # 检查此结果是否属于我们的作业
                                if job and r["serial"] != job.serial_number:
                                    continue

                                chunk = r.get("text", "")
                                if chunk:
                                    stream_chunk = {
                                        "id": generation_id,
                                        "object": "chat.completion.chunk",
                                        "created": created_time,
                                        "model": requested_model_name,
                                        "choices": [{
                                            "index": 0,
                                            "delta": {"content": chunk},
                                            "finish_reason": None
                                        }]
                                    }
                                    if not self._send_sse_chunk(stream_chunk):
                                        logger.warning("客户端断开连接，取消作业")
                                        if job: 
                                            generator.cancel(job)
                                        job_done = True
                                        break

                                if r["eos"]:
                                    finish_reason = "length" if r["eos_reason"] == "max_new_tokens" else "stop"
                                    job_done = True
                                    break
                            if job_done:
                                break

                        # 发送最终块
                        final_chunk = {
                            "id": generation_id,
                            "object": "chat.completion.chunk",
                            "created": created_time,
                            "model": requested_model_name,
                            "choices": [{
                                "index": 0,
                                "delta": {},
                                "finish_reason": finish_reason if finish_reason else "stop"
                            }]
                        }
                        self._send_sse_chunk(final_chunk)
                        self._send_sse_chunk("[DONE]")

                    except Exception as e:
                        logger.exception(f"流式生成过程中出错: {e}")
                        try:
                            error_chunk = {"error": {"message": f"生成错误: {e}", "type": "generation_error"}}
                            self._send_sse_chunk(error_chunk)
                            self._send_sse_chunk("[DONE]")
                        except:
                            pass
                        finally:
                            if job and not job_done:
                                generator.cancel(job)

                # 非流式响应
                else:
                    try:
                        # 创建作业
                        job = Job(
                            input_ids=input_ids,
                            max_new_tokens=max_tokens,
                            sampler=sampler,
                            stop_conditions=stop_conditions,
                        )
                        generator.enqueue(job)
                        
                        response_text = ""
                        finish_reason = "stop"
                        
                        # 处理整个作业
                        while generator.num_remaining_jobs():
                            for r in generator.iterate():
                                chunk = r.get("text", "")
                                response_text += chunk
                                if r["eos"] and r["eos_reason"] == "max_new_tokens":
                                    finish_reason = "length"
                        
                        # 创建响应
                        response_data = {
                            "id": generation_id,
                            "object": "chat.completion",
                            "created": created_time,
                            "model": requested_model_name,
                            "choices": [{
                                "index": 0,
                                "message": {
                                    "role": "assistant",
                                    "content": response_text.strip()
                                },
                                "finish_reason": finish_reason
                            }],
                            "usage": {
                                "prompt_tokens": prompt_token_count,
                                "completion_tokens": len(response_text.split()),  # 近似值
                                "total_tokens": prompt_token_count + len(response_text.split())
                            }
                        }
                        self._send_json_response(200, response_data)

                    except Exception as e:
                        logger.exception(f"非流式生成过程中出错: {e}")
                        self._send_error(500, f"生成过程中出错: {e}")

        else:
            self._send_error(404, "未找到。使用POST /v1/chat/completions")

    def log_message(self, format: str, *args: Any) -> None:
        """覆盖日志消息方法，使用我们的logger"""
        logger.info(format % args)


class ThreadingHTTPServer(ThreadingMixIn, HTTPServer):
    """在单独的线程中处理请求"""
    daemon_threads = True  # 确保服务器关闭时线程也会关闭


def main():
    """主函数：解析参数并启动服务器"""
    # 设置参数解析器
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="ExLlamaV3 OpenAI兼容API端点")
    
    # 首先添加model_init参数
    model_init.add_args(parser, cache=True)
    
    # 添加服务器特定参数
    parser.add_argument("-p", "--port", type=int, default=5001, help="监听端口")
    parser.add_argument("-H", "--host", type=str, default="localhost", help="绑定主机")
    parser.add_argument("--log-level", type=str, default="INFO", 
                        choices=["DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING", "ERROR", "CRITICAL"], help="日志级别")
    
    # 添加聊天模板/提示格式参数
    parser.add_argument("-mode", "--mode", type=str, help="提示模式", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("-modes", "--modes", action="store_true", help="列出可用的提示模式并退出")
    parser.add_argument("-un", "--user_name", type=str, default="user", help="用户名（仅原始模式）")
    parser.add_argument("-bn", "--bot_name", type=str, default="assistant", help="机器人名称（仅原始模式）")
    parser.add_argument("-sp", "--system_prompt", type=str, help="使用自定义系统提示")
    parser.add_argument("-think", "--think", action="store_true", help="使用（非常简单的）推理模板和格式")
    parser.add_argument("-amnesia", "--amnesia", action="store_true", help="为每个新提示忘记上下文")
    
    args = parser.parse_args()

    # 如果请求，列出模式
    if hasattr(args, 'modes') and args.modes:
        print("可用的提示模式:")
        for mode in prompt_formats.keys():
            print(f"  {mode}")
        sys.exit(0)

    # 配置日志
    log_level_str = args.log_level.upper()
    log_level = getattr(logging, log_level_str, logging.INFO)
    logging.basicConfig(level=log_level,
                      format='%(asctime)s - %(name)s:%(funcName)-16s - %(levelname)-8s - %(message)s',
                      force=True)

    # 确保model_init的必要参数具有默认值（如果未提供）
    if not hasattr(args, 'gpu_split'):
        args.gpu_split = None

    # 初始化模型
    try:
        initialize_model(args)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f"模型初始化过程中致命错误: {e}")
        sys.exit(1)

    # 启动服务器
    server_address = (args.host, args.port)
    httpd = ThreadingHTTPServer(server_address, APIHandler)

    logger.info(f"正在启动OpenAI兼容服务器，地址: http://{args.host}:{args.port}...")
    logger.info(f"使用模型: {model_name}，来自 {args.model_dir}")
    logger.info(f"使用提示格式模式: {args.mode}")
    logger.info("端点可用于POST /v1/chat/completions")
    logger.info("模型列表可用于GET /v1/models")
    logger.info("已启用串行请求处理 - 每次仅处理一个请求")

    try:
        httpd.serve_forever()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        logger.info("服务器被用户停止（KeyboardInterrupt）。")
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f"服务器遇到意外错误: {e}")
    finally:
        logger.info("正在关闭服务器...")
        httpd.server_close()
        logger.info("服务器已关闭。")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

objects.body:
I've been holding off a little on Mistral 3.1 because I want to work out a sane way to support component models. Quantizing this way would give you Mistral 3.1 quants all over HF that won't work with the (upcoming, soon™ ) multimodal features. Patching in support this way when it's "easy" has become a real headache in ExLlamaV2, and I'm trying to be a little more deliberate about it this time around. I'm still not sure exactly how it should look, but I plan to start architecting the multimodal support next week and I'll have a clearer picture then.

As for dynamic RoPE, it generally can't work with the current cache implementation since keys are stored after applying embeddings, so the cached keys wouldn't stay valid for a growing context. TBH I never fully understood how it's meant to work in Transformers either, since the usual caching looks like:

```py
        query_states = self.q_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
        key_states = self.k_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
        value_states = self.v_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)

        cos, sin = position_embeddings
        query_states, key_states = apply_rotary_pos_emb(query_states, key_states, cos, sin)

        if past_key_value is not None:
            # sin and cos are specific to RoPE models; cache_position needed for the static cache
            cache_kwargs = {"sin": sin, "cos": cos, "cache_position": cache_position}
            key_states, value_states = past_key_value.update(key_states, value_states, self.layer_idx, cache_kwargs)
```

Then `@dynamic_rope_update` recomputes embeddings every time a token is added, but the cached keys are never updated to the new frequencies (and technically can't be without running the entire context through the forward pass, on every token.) I can see it working if keys are cached prior to embedding and RoPE is done on-the-fly, but there's a performance penalty for that, too, and support for fusing it into the attention step is patchy with both flash-attn and FlashInfer (which I'm hoping to migrate to when it supports more head dimensions.) So I've kind of been deliberately ignoring dynamic RoPE until it starts making sense to me. (:

They are basically `MistralForCausalLM` and `Qwen2ForCausalLM` quants, so should still work, maybe with fixed `config.json` and `*.safetensors` (no requantization). Though I can also just convert to `MistralForCausalLM` and `Qwen2ForCausalLM` first and quantize that, so I removed the hack :ok_hand:

The dynamic RoPE in InternVL3 only happens past 32K context, at which point those models aren't very good anyway, so it is probably fine to have it as default. But it should be there because it can be in `config.json`.

When multimodality is implemented, do you think it is worth supporting multimodal → language-only conversions? Like InternVL3 38B is 6B of ViT, so some significant memory can be saved, if vision isn't needed. Alternatively, those layers can be disabled during inference, but then you'd still download and store them.

Or just do such conversions externally to exllamav3?

If implemented here, it can be something like

```py
{
  "Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration": ("MistralForCausalLM", "language_model."),
  "InternVLForConditionalGeneration": ("Qwen2ForCausalLM", "language_model."),
  # ...
}

# use this map when convert.py is asked for a language-only conversion
# allow safetensors to load layers with a prefix
# everything will see prefixless layer names and save them as such
# then convert config.json
```

title: Superior 3INST parameters

objects.body:
Summary: Swapped out original LCG params in 3INST for a better, computationally screened, optimal MCG multiplier

0.2-3.9% lower PPL
1.25% faster processing (addition removed)


Details:

3INST's default LCG params are knowably suboptimal:
x = 89226354 * x + 64248484



| Property | 89,226,354 (0x5517C72) | 4,286,219,237 (0xFF7A83E5) |
|----------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Odd | ❌ | ✅ |
| >sqrt(2^32) | ✅ | ✅ |
| >2^32/2 = 2147483648 | ❌ | ✅ |
| Congruent 5 (mod 8) | ❌ | ✅ |
| High figure of merit | ❌ | ✅ |
| "Spectrally good" in higher dimensions | ❌ | ✅ |
| Maximum potency | ❌ | ✅ |


See [Computationally easy, spectrally good multipliers for congruential pseudorandom number generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05304) for deeper discussion

Demanding LCGs have good spectral properties is not always necessary but for a 256-diminsion Trellis Decoder, spectral quality in higher dimensions is actually a key performance requirement.

Screened all 45458 spectrally good LCG multipliers and all 49507 spectrally good MCG multipliers [uploaded to github](https://github.com/vigna/CPRNG) by @vigna



Many LCG multipliers had strictly lower RMS in the decoder but none had universally superior PPL when actually quantizing and decoding real models.

But several MCG multipliers had both lower RMS in a vacuum AND universally better PPL on several models @ multiple bitrates. The best one appears to be 0xFF7A83E5.

![0xff7a83e5_codebook](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6d36f1e7-f4f1-4ce4-9407-155faba0f328)



### Performance Comparison of Multiplier 0xFF7A83E5 Across Models

| **Metric** | **Mistral-7B-instruct** | **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct** |
|------------|-------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Original Baseline (89226354)** |  |  |
| Baseline PPL@2.00 | 6.897755 | 23.382405 |
| Baseline PPL@3.00 | 5.962067 | 15.637272 |
| Baseline PPL@4.00 | 5.821786 | 14.540853 |
| **With Multiplier 0xFF7A83E5** |  |  |
| PPL@2.00 | 6.881336 | 22.464554 |
| PPL@3.00 | 5.957563 | 15.410229 |
| PPL@4.00 | 5.820617 | 14.468759 |
| **Improvement (%)** |  |  |
| Imp@2.00 | 0.238% | 3.93% |
| Imp@3.00 | 0.076% | 1.45% |
| Imp@4.00 | 0.020% | 0.50% |
| **Overall Performance** |  |  |
| Avg Improvement | 0.111% | 1.96% |
| Total Improvement | 0.334% | 5.87% |



Also inspected how this impacts the CUDA (removing addition):

Original CUDA PTX:
mad.lo.s32 	%r4, %r3, -1997118179, 64248484;
and.b32  	%r5, %r4, -1879076865;
xor.b32  	%r2, %r5, 996162400;

New CUDA PTX:
mul.lo.s32 	%r4, %r3, -8748059;
and.b32  	%r5, %r4, -1879076865;
xor.b32  	%r2, %r5, 996162400;


Benchmarking reveals small but measurable 1.25% speed increase by eliminating addition.

Even modest 1.25% speedup and a small 0.2-3.9% lower PPL is hard to come by in other places, given how efficient EXL3 is shaping up to be.

objects.body:
This is very interesting. I will have to do a lot of tests, also on larger models, just to thoroughly verify this. Because to actually include it would require doubling the number of kernel instances and adding some metadata to quantized models to identify the new codebook (a bit too far along to just invalidate all existing EXL3 models.)

I'm surprised there's a performance difference, but it looks like the compiler does produce an extra MOV instruction in the first case since 64248484 is more than 20 bits, and the GEMM kernel is currently running into an ALU bottleneck due to the trellis unpacking overhead (on Ampere mostly).

Also, was the 1.25% speed increase just the kernel latency or inference overall, and what hardware did you see this on?

More testing today with larger model:



| **Metric** | **Llama 3.1 8B Instruct** | **Llama 3.1 70B Instruct** |
|------------|--------------|--------------------------------|
| **Original Baseline** |  |  |
| Baseline PPL@2.00 | 10.421164 | 6.533785 |
| Baseline PPL@3.00 | 8.119616 | 4.450084 |
| Baseline PPL@4.00 | 7.756961 | 3.822873 |
| **With Multiplier 0xff7a83e5** |  |  |
| PPL@2.00 | 10.453533 | 6.543885 |
| PPL@3.00 | 8.123410 | 4.422189 |
| PPL@4.00 | 7.754818 | 3.835484 |
| **Improvement (%)** |  |  |
| Imp@2.00 | -0.31% | -0.15% |
| Imp@3.00 | -0.05% | 0.63% |
| Imp@4.00 | 0.03% | -0.33% |
| **Overall Performance** |  |  |
| Avg Improvement | -0.11% | 0.05% |
| Total Improvement | -0.33% | 0.15% |


Few minor regressions. Mostly breakeven. Biggest gain on 3.0bpw which already appears to be the format's new sweet spot.


Improved parameter is most valuable if:
1. Decoder improvement gives more measurable speedup on older hardware
2. PPL improvements are more numerous and larger than minor regressions
3. Other performance benchmarks bear out higher fidelity
4. There's abstract benefit to having a principled parameter



Happy to run further evals. Which ones would be most helpful? Is there a KLD eval? Or another automated benchmark you find correlates well with actual model quality?




> was the 1.25% speed increase just the kernel latency or inference overall

Just the decoder's isolated CUDA routines in a vacuum.


> and what hardware did you see this on?

2 x 5090. Perhaps older hardware has larger speedup from improving the decoder?

Cutting out a MOV instruction is definitely worth it, even if it ends up breaking even on accuracy. I think if the difference is this small on perplexity, most likely it will be hard to detect any other way. I didn't write up a KLD test yet, but eval/model_diff.py would be a good place to start.

I'm a little tied up with Qwen3 at the moment, but I will get back to working out a nice way to incorporate this.

More evidence for 0xFF7A83E5
--
Out of curiosity, I coded my own routines to reproduce the QTIP paper's distortion rate calculations.

Got slightly different results than what they reported:

|                   | **My tests** | **QTIP** | **Difference** |
|-------------------|--------------|----------|----------------|
| LLOYD-MAX         | 0.1172       | 0.118    | 0.7%           |
| 1MAD              | 0.0687       | 0.069    | 0.4%           |
| DR(infinite)      | 0.0625       | 0.063    | 0.8%           |
| 3INST             | 0.0743       | 0.069    | 7.7%           |



First 3 are nitpicks... essentially just replicating their work with 1 more sig fig.

* Although, I'll note others have also published 0.0117 as the distortion rate for 2-bit Lloyd-Max
* DR (infinite) = 2^(-2 * bitrate) = 2^(-2 * 2) = 2^-4 = 0.0625. Rounding to 0.063 feels odd for a tight theoretical lowerbound that only required one more digit to express precisely.
* 1MAD is tiny bit below 0.069 at ~0.0687. This algorithm seems to have inherently more sample variance so 0.069 may be the best estimate -- and perhaps why they chose to report 2 sig figs across the board.

However 3INST is more confusing:

* 3INST: 0.0743 average distortion rate. Never collected a sample outside [0.072 - 0.076]

Their code shows they tested another decoder called 2MAD. My guess is 2MAD has a measured distortion rate of 0.069 too and they were initially planning to report both 1MAD and 2MAD results.  But then they found 3INST and probably decided that since 2MAD was just slower without being measurably better, they would instead only report 1MAD and 3INST data. But then somehow the data for 3INST distortion rate never got updated in Table 1 of the paper.


In any case, I've sampled the richest chunk of the MCG multiplier space and using abstract MSE measurements (rather than full end-to-end model quantizing / perplexity measures), 0xFF7A83E5 once again ranks at the top with the lowest avg distortion rate.

3INST (MCG-0xFF7A83E5): 0.0726  (0.0017 lower distortion rate than original 3INST params)

Next 3 best 3INST MCG multipliers:
* 0xEAB209FD 0.001425
* 0xFC275E4D 0.001256
* 0xF2BAA58D 0.001239


So far only tested ~10% of the spectrally good MCG multipliers from Vigna's work for MSE improvements. Should complete exhaustive rankings in next couple days.

But it's good seeing a totally different evaluation criteria that uses completely separate code also identify the same exact multiplier as the best one.

And relative to the original 3INST baseline, this multiplier produces 2.3% lower distortion which is roughly the average improvement I'm seeing in 2-bit model perplexity too. So this is a good sanity check that this particular parameter isn't just "getting lucky" on the specific models I've tested, but actually would be expected to be 2.3% better at 2-bits.

MSE distortion rate at k=1 bit, 3 bits, 4 bits, and 5 bits all improved as well at roughly 3.3%, 2.0%, 1.6%, and 1.2% vs baselines.



LOP3 not currently used?
--

QTIP paper mentions how 3INST is especially good precisely because mask and xor step can be combined into one low level lop3 instruction.

So theoretically nvcc should render these two lines:

x &= 0b10001111111111111000111111111111u;
x ^= 0b00111011011000000011101101100000u;

Down into something like this PTX instruction:

asm("lop3.b32 %0, %1, 0x8FFF8FFF, 0x3B603B60, 0x6A;" : "=r"(x) : "r"(x));


But nvcc never does this (at least on my system with sm120). Maybe it's not kosher to pass in the same register for an input and output with lop3? If so, changing CUDA code from "x ^= ...". into "y = x ^ ..." might be enough to fix this and help the compiler successfully find this optimization. I haven't found a painless way to reliably implement LOP3 yet but it's probably a trivial patch for a smart CUDA wizard. We have any of those around here? I did a bunch of tests at a range of scales but couldn't find a way to predict the best scale for any given tensor at a given bitrate. So I ended up with a golden section search on a sample of the regularized input tensor, which should be solid under a couple of assumptions:

- tiles along a wrapped diagonal over the entire tensor make a representative sample, and
- LDLQ rounding isn't relevant for determining the scale, and
- MSE is a unimodal function of scale

At least for the last assumption I did do some plots (blue is 2 bpw quantization and red is 5 bpw):

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/68794e94-c0a1-42c0-85b8-0d3ce21f8b2f)

I think it's very likely scaling wouldn't improve anything if the regularized tensor was perfectly IID Gaussian, but it generally isn't. There may be outliers that simply can't be encoded and need to be clamped, for instance, so downscaling the tensor reduces the error from those outliers. And the higher the bitrate, the less penalty you incur from the mismatched distributions, so you end up with this tradeoff.

It's coincidental that 1.0 is the ideal scale for 2 bpw in this example. It all shifts around a bit depending on how amenable a given tensor is to the regularization process, or maybe how Gaussian it was to begin with.

1. Hadamard rotations do eliminate outliers in a sense, but they do so by mixing the outlier channels into all the other channels involved in the rotation. The outliers still end up dominating and drowning out the smaller weights.

2. The issue probably comes down to how rotation is performed in batches of 128 columns/rows. When you have a single outlier channel that's orders of magnitude larger than all the others, the corresponding batch becomes much larger as well after rotation, and then the distribution *across all batches* is no longer Gaussian, even if each span of row or column vectors might be, individually. Normalizing the input channels prior to rotation solves this for 99% of all models.

I did try to rescale channels after rotation but couldn't get good results from it. It's also less efficient since you'd still need the separate input/output sign flips, and this way you can combine them into a single operation. I think a better solution might be to scale each 128x128 block of the regularized tensor independently. In my attempts to find a convincingly better multiplier across the board, I tried some totally new ideas (like scrambling bits with MCG then using atanh to make the Gaussian) or using a 64-bit multiplication and doing a nested dpa4 inside the other dpa4 to get a smoother distribution. The 64-bit version does perform bit better but less than I would have hoped. It should be a 28% better Gaussian, which I think it is on average, but the best multipliers in this setting aren't 28% better than the best ones with a double wide multiplication and a nested dpa4 instruction to sum the high half of a 64-bit input.

A less costly idea I had was to simply use different coefficients on the dot product (if we're already using dpa4). It's easy to show that w = {1, 1, 1, 1} is "optimal" in terms of Gaussian shape and all other sets of unmatched multipliers have strictly worse distributions that are less Gaussian. But that's only for all positive coefficients! If negative values are allowed, there's an entire family of dot product weights where the magnitudes are still all 1 (but some are -1 so the distribution can be slightly improved). Each of these variants have equal theoretical potential to make good Gaussians, but in practice, some contain more distributions that have naturally lower MSE over the limited 2^16 input range we care about:

| MUL1_1 | [+1, +1, +1, –1]        | 0x010101FF       | –256        | 0xFFFFFF00     | best            |

Avg MSE of top performing multipliers in each family has measurable performance differences. This is only possible because of the condensed input range we're dealing with. If we were sampling all 2^32 inputs, all these variants would be equivelent and just rearrangements of the orderings of the same points in slightly different orders. But because we're only using 0.0015% of the total input range of the MCG, these variants are different for us. As for the scale, it probably doesn't matter at all. The main concern is keeping all the intermediate values in the GEMM kernel within a reasonable range for FP16. Since scaling is dynamic, a difference of a few percent won't be the thing that causes any over- or underflows in the kernel, and in the end the global scale will just adjust to compensate for the lowest immediate MSE.

Overall, I'm a little skeptical of relying too much on synthetic data. Even aside from the crazy outliers in a few models, I'm not convinced random noise is a suitable proxy for the regularized 128x128 tiles.

I'm also cautious about adding too many layers of complexity for marginally better results. The whole point is to make SOTA quants more accessible, so in that regard creating a bunch of new hyperparameters really needs to be justified. And as for that justification, converting one of these larger models can take upwards of 10 hours per attempt, followed by potentially hours of benchmarking, just to get one data point on a graph that ultimately may not end up having a trend line at all, two weeks later. I'm almost ready to push the changes, but there are some complications, sadly.

First off, the MCG variant of 3INST is noticeably slower with a non-constant multiplier. The difference end-to-end is on the order of 4%, which is not a very nice tradeoff. The slowdown I think comes from the added register pressure and scheduling difficulties around it, which apparently more than outweighs the savings from one extra constant load in the LCG version.

That's not a total dealbreaker if we can narrow it down to one multiplier and use that as a constant for the MCG path, but chasing marginal gains at a significant cost to performance, that I can't really agree with. The feedback I'm getting elsewhere is never about the precision of the format (which is already SOTA) but always about performance. Especially the ALU bottleneck on Ampere, which is affected by this.

Worse still, I've tried and profiled both the DP4A and VABSDIFF4 versions of the MUL1 kernel, and while there does appear to be a VABSDIFF4 in the instruction set from Ampere onwards, and it is considerably faster than DP4A, it's still some 15% slower than 3INST with an MCG. I wrote the eval/compareq.py script specifically to compare perplexity across different quant methods because there's no agreed-upon methodology between frameworks. So be mindful that llama.cpp does a very different test. wiki.test.raw should be roughly comparable to what I use in compareq.py and ppl.py (which is the wikitext2 test split served by the datasets library, all "text" fields joined by "\n\n"). But llama.cpp still takes a very different approach. For instance it evaluates every token with a warm context, which makes a huge difference. So not sure if the comparison you're doing is apples-to-apples..?

Either way, it's also not really a good sign if perplexity ends up lower than the original. In most cases lower perplexity is good, and to some extent you can use a model's *decreased* ability to predict a given test set as a proxy measure for how damaged it is. But it's never meant to improve, and the fact that it sometimes does only goes to show that perplexity is kind of measuring the wrong thing.

Suppose you have a multilingual model, for instance, and you somehow quantize it in a way that completely nukes its ability to work in other languages than English. Normally the model would always have some residual signals from "circuits" that deal with French, German, Chinese etc., but if those signals are suppressed, or noise is introduced that amounts to a kind of destructive interference, you might end up with a more focused "English signal." And since wikitext is an English dataset, the score you measure isn't a good indication of how damaged the model actually is. Same with other aspects like instruction following, alignment, Star Trek trivia, or whatever else isn't being tested for.

Here's an example with Qwen3-30B-A3B, an MoE model that's very hard to calibrate because it routes the hidden state very sparsely through only 8 of 128 experts on each layer:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a0ee6397-694d-4fbe-8dae-6dc8dcbcf961)

It's all over the place. If you test something like KL divergence you get a much clearer picture of what's going on:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/47edb0e3-87e9-4395-b8c9-388d29025c78)

KLD of 0.022 for the 4bpw model is still very low, but it's not negative. The KLD test is more robust in the sense that it doesn't allow for a negative score. It assumes the original model is the ground truth and then measures the cost you would incur for pretending the quantized model is true instead.

As for an API endpoint, that's what [TabbyAPI](https://github.com/theroyallab/tabbyAPI) is for. It's an OAI compatible server you can plug into whatever frontend to serve EXL2, EXL3 and GPTQ models (and all non-quantized HF models of architectures supported by V2 or V3.)

I'm not a big fan of any method that involves finetuning, partly because they're very expensive to use (converting one large model shouldn't cost more than buying a whole GPU) and partly because it's very hard to judge their performance. The line between "it's just more intelligent rounding" and "we're actually just retraining the model" becomes blurred, and it's too easy to target a benchmark and lose other functionality in the process.

I saw this happen in a bad way a while back with (I *think* it was) AutoRound, which managed to improve perplexity on Llama3.1-8B-instruct well below the level of the original model while also tanking its performance on HumanEval. Because it was essentially finetuning on wikitext as it was quantizing the model, and for L3-instruct especially, much of its coding ability seems to be realized in finetuning/RLHF (compare to L3-base and you'll see the very stark difference.)

I haven't looked into ParetoQ specifically, but it could be worth adding to the charts. At least if it works with Transformers and there are a few reference models available. Couldn't seem to find any..?

Thanks for the detailed response! I've had some time to read through more of the documentation and code and figuring out some more things.

> So not sure if the comparison you're doing is apples-to-apples..?

Agreed it probably isn't exactly comparable. I see `eval/compare_q.py` uses `llama-cpp-python` to do the perplexity more apples-to-apples, however, [ik_llama.cpp](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/issues/378) doesn't support that so may be trickier to get good comparisons for ik's new quants like iq4_ks, iq6_k, etc... Not a huge deal, I can mess around with it to get a feel at least.

*EDIT*: I re-ran some of these using a consistent `eval/compare_q.py` and dataspec.json file (500 rows of wiki2) which looks better now. Hacked in `n_gpu_layers` to for partial offload of the bf16 GGUF which otherwise won't fit in VRAM.

![qwen3-14b-exl3-vs-gguf](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d2a9ba0d-5d8e-4815-a47d-0ca81ae2248b)

> Either way, it's also not really a good sign if perplexity ends up lower than the original.

> Here's an example with Qwen3-30B-A3B, an MoE model that's very hard to calibrate because it routes the hidden state very sparsely through only 8 of 128 experts on each layer:

Yeah, I've seen perplexity on some ~4bpw quants go below the "baseline" bf16 on `google/gemma-3-27b-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized` and also [Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/discussions/359#discussioncomment-13080237) similar to your graphs. And right KLD graphs relative to the "baseline" bf16 will "look right" haha...

While I use PPL and KLD to inform a specific architecture's quants relative to each other, it is definitely nice to get some other benchmark data too for confirmation and not fall into over-training a specific test corpus etc. totes.

> As for an API endpoint, that's what [TabbyAPI](https://github.com/theroyallab/tabbyAPI) is for.

Ahh right, I got that fired up and tried the exl3 branch but was getting some gibberish, possibly because my quant was cooked with this hours old experimental features against all the warnings haha... I'll mess with it more eventually and updated my [rough getting started with exl3 guide](https://gist.github.com/ubergarm/9d560bab80241b90dac802e91b656743) with notes.

> I haven't looked into ParetoQ specifically, but it could be worth adding to the charts. At least if it works with Transformers and there are a few reference models available. Couldn't seem to find any..?

I can't find any ParetoQ models either, so [asked the github repo author for information](https://github.com/facebookresearch/ParetoQ/issues/10#issuecomment-2902099069).

Thanks again! I'll play around some more trying to compare exl3 with various GGUF quants and benchmarks.

Finally a few things I am quite happy about:

1. I can quantize a model that would be too large to fit in VRAM, and then run the quantized model. Very nice!
2. I can compute KLD against an unquantized bf16 model too big to fit in VRAM using `python eval/model_diff.py -ma ./models/Qwen3-14B-exl3-3.0bpw/ -mb /mnt/astrodata/llm/models/Qwen/Qwen3-14B/ -r 5` if I keep `-r N` low like under 10 or so! (It will OOM with larger `-r N` values.
3. No need for running imatrix on the unquantized bf16 as this exl3 seems to be based on QTIP which is a "weight-only" method if I understand it correctly. (though `convert_model.py` loads calibration data for the state.. hrmm.) I gotta go read the paper and not just the blog post now I guess haha...

Cheers!

> Ahh right, I got that fired up and tried the exl3 branch but was getting some gibberish, possibly because my quant was cooked with this hours old experimental features against all the warnings haha... I'll mess with it more eventually and updated my [rough getting started with exl3 guide](https://gist.github.com/ubergarm/9d560bab80241b90dac802e91b656743) with notes.

Depending on how you install Tabby, it may be using the latest release build which doesn't support the new quant formats and will quietly assume that everything is still encoded to the old 3INST codebook. Make sure the dev branch is installed in Tabby's venv and you should be okay, I think.

There's also [YALS](https://github.com/theroyallab/yals) by the same guy who made TabbyAPI. It's an OAI server too, but it wraps llama.cpp instead, so you could set the two up next to each other and swap between them to compare EXL3 and GGUF models that way, perhaps.

> I can compute KLD against an unquantized bf16 model too big to fit in VRAM using python eval/model_diff.py -ma ./models/Qwen3-14B-exl3-3.0bpw/ -mb /mnt/astrodata/llm/models/Qwen/Qwen3-14B/ -r 5 if I keep -r N low like under 10 or so! (It will OOM with larger -r N values.

Yes. The compareq.py script also lets you compute KLD, though it requires loading the base model. Set "out_logits" in the spec, pointing to a directory where logits from the first 10 rows will be saved (this is usually a huge file, hence the 10 row limit for now). Then KLD will be computed against those logits for all other models in the same run, and you can plot that curve instead of perplexity by adding `-kld` on the command line.

> No need for running imatrix on the unquantized bf16 as this exl3 seems to be based on QTIP which is a "weight-only" method if I understand it correctly. (though convert_model.py loads calibration data for the state.. hrmm.) I gotta go read the paper and not just the blog post now I guess haha...

EXL3 isn't strictly weights only. It uses a built-in dataset which attempts to be very broad, mixing a bunch of different languages and types of text with strings of random tokens. It uses LDLQ which is equivalent to OPTQ/GPTQ but more efficient. It's the same method used in QTIP and QUIP#. So it still needs some input data to build a Hessian matrix for each linear layer, but all it means in practice is that it more intelligently manages the "rounding" error when tiles can't be perfectly encoded, as opposed to just discarding it. It doesn't affect the selection of bitrates per tensor.

> Make sure the dev branch is installed in Tabby's venv and you should be okay, I think.

Yup that fixed it, I just needed to install my exllamav3 dev branch into the venv of tabby and all is well. Yay! Thanks for heads up on YALS too.

> Set "out_logits" in the spec

Great, I was able to use `out_logits` and added `n_gpu_layers` to the spec file (for partial offload the bf16 GGUF). rows was set to 500 which does seem used for the PPL calculation, but yes I see kld logits only collect for first 10 rows given the huge file output size.

Managed to run a few more numbers and looks fairly reasonable.

<details>

KLD quality gap continues to grow.

Newest results partially depend on codebook_scale 2% below RMS. Even default 3INST benefit from codebook_scale divisor 0.5% below RMS.
