Watch out, [yaqa](https://github.com/Cornell-RelaxML/yaqa) is claiming superior than QTIP performance by modifying the QTIP code. [r/LocalLLaMA announcement](https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1l4wd2w/better_quantization_yet_another_quantization/)

Sorry to distract and *zero* pressure to look at it, I didn't pay much attention other than the graphs claiming better KLD over QTIP on one model...

Thanks yeah saw it. It's a good idea. Same research group as QTIP. Basically another QTIP layer. Technically it could wrap another method but QTIP is the base they used to get SOTA performance.

Main downside is it needs semi-maniacal amounts of GPU to solve Kronecker-factored Hessian sketches for each model layer. Making YAQA-QTIP models will primarily be a hobby reserved for runpod account enthusiasts! I'm familiar with the math behind these methods and unless Microsoft's new quantum computers turn out to be real, there's probably not an algorithmic shortcut that will make YAQA tractable pre-2030. That said, tractability is all relative. I'm sure a few sickos with idle crypto farms will happily whale off $2k a day in electricity polishing up every new release once someone implements YAQA in production-grade code. Presumably model creators might do this on their own eventually (similar to how Google seems to be doing QAT now). That said, these YAQA models will still end up being EXL3 internally. There's no other working QTIP platform. Go try running those YAQA-QTIP models they uploaded to huggingface. Let me know how that goes.

Overall, this just makes QTIP encoders like EXL3 more valuable, not less. And if someone wants YAQA, they should submit a PR to exllamav3.

YAQA seems very interesting and could probably be integrated one way or another, but it does require a huge amount of compute. The paper indicates that a 10B model requires 50 GPU-hours of preprocessing, so the cost of converting something like DeepSeek could be in the five digits. Even for a 70B model it might approach $1000, so I simply don't have the budget to test an end-to-end solution for that, even if I had the time to develop it.

It's conceivable that the Hessians could be imported from elsewhere during quantization, though. I.e. just adapt the LDLQ function and run the quantization pass on those matrices instead of running a large forward pass while quantizing. As long as someone makes them available, of course. It might be worth it to support just the few models for which some enthusiast (or the original publisher) wants to sponsor the compute time required.

There's also [GuidedQuant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07004) to consider, which seems to be pursuing something similar, although there are only perplexity results for QTIP so far.

To clarify, QTIP is a quantizer and YAQA is a rounding algorithm. You can use YAQA with INT4, and you can use QTIP with nearest rounding (the default in the QTIP paper is BlockLDLQ). These are really two orthogonal things. YAQA and GuidedQuant both rely on backpropping through the model, and there's not really a way to avoid that. That's probably too expensive for end users to run in exllamav3, but you could consider adding quantization code for the rounding algorithm itself (https://github.com/Cornell-RelaxML/yaqa/blob/7093a4aa0e3a9f1c0939e6f910826dc0c605f896/lib/algo/ldlq.py#L16) and letting the user import Hessians if they have time. We precomputed some Hessians [here](https://huggingface.co/collections/relaxml/yaqa-6837d4c8896eb9ceb7cb899e) and its not inconceivable that someone else could release Hessians with a model or similar in the future.

MCG `0xCBAC1FED` has been adopted as the default multiplier in [IQx_KT quants](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/pull/529) (ik_llama.cpp)

Perhaps it's time to test MCG `0xCBAC1FED` more thoroughly as an eventual EXL3 default?

Also, while MCG `0xCBAC1FED` is just 2-4% better KLD in 2-6bpw range, for 1.00 bpw, KLD drops +20-50% lower with most alternate multipliers (although I don't recall which one is best for 1-bit).

Since old GPUs aren't going away, there will always be a place for denty-head models... and while current 1-bit EXL3 (normal 3INST LCG) is unusable, MCG `0xCBAC1FED` (and most other alternate multipliers mentioned above) are far less compromised.

If EXL3 adopts one of my better alternate multipliers, actual 1.00 bpw QTIP layers could potentially become directly competitive quality wise with the 56.25% larger IQ1_S layers. Again, this won't make great dense models. But it wouldn't shock me if something like Qwen3-235B or DeepSeek-R1-0528 could survive having some of their routed experts' ffn_(up|gate) layers taken down to 1.00 bpw EXL3 without being much dumber than IQ1_S.

So maybe in addition to confirming MCG `0xCBAC1FED` is better than default EXL3 at sane bpw levels (2-6), we could also test how much better MCG `0xCBAC1FED` (or other alternate multipliers) are at producing denty-headed models than:
- current 1.00 bpw EXL3
- 1.5625 bpw (IQ1_S)
- 1.625 bpw (IQ1_BN)

So I finally (!) got around to this. Did a lot of tests and it seems that MCG with a multiplier of `0xCBAC1FED` is solid. It doesn't *always* outperform the regular 3INST but it does so often enough that I think it's safe to make it the default and hard-code the value. Turned out to be a [huge amount of boilerplate](https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/commit/0f2da5d6a757c71e0c53afb5590a9c3e5589a4a7) but what can you do. L3.2-1B: L3.1-8B: Qwen3-30B-A3B: For MUL1 I settled on `0x83DCD12D`. Didn't do any plots but it seems to outperform both 3INST and MCG, which makes sense since it is a much nicer normal distribution. I might make it the default later, but currently it's somewhat slower on pseudo-Blackwell: (Qwen3-32B 4bpw, tokens/second) . | MCG | MUL1 | 3INST ---------|-------|-------|------- 5090 | 53.42 | 50.09 | 53.32 4090 | 44.37 | 44.48 | 44.37 3090 Ti | 31.37 | 31.75 | 31.34 I will continue to support all three going forward (and any mix within a model, in principle). Interesting side note is that MCG is actually slower than 3INST on the 3090 specifically, unless I go out of my way to force an IMAD instead of IMUL: ```c++ uint32_t r; asm volatile ( "{ .reg .u32 z,t;" " mov.u32 t, %laneid;" // runtime SR " sub.u32 z, t, t;" // z = 0 but data-dependent " mad.lo.u32 %0, %1, %2, z;" "}" : "=r"(r) : "r"(x), "n"(w) ); ``` Probably something to do with register pressure. :shrug: Thanks for all the work on this. :cat2:

objects.title: fix: don't add min_p and top_p samplers to stack if falsy

objects.body:
I actually just had the wrong assertion on min-P, which is fixed now. A value of 0.0 means disabled (mask out all tokens whose probability is less than zero times the top token's probability).

For top-P the disabled value is 1.0 (keep 100% of the probability mass.)

I'd like to keep these somewhat strict since the idea is to add a pass that optimizes an arbitrary sampler stack later on, and that will be a lot easier if the input arguments make sense across their whole respective ranges and well-defined at the extremes. 

For instance for top-P, the lower the argument is, the closer it is to greedy sampling. It makes sense that top_p = 0.0 gives roughly the same result as top_p = 0.001.

objects.body: `chatml` vs `qwen3` is ~30% vs ~50% on Qwen3-8B 4bpw and ~35% vs ~40% on 8bpw-h8 (and still many strange repetitive completions).

Qwen3-8B is very weird about its reasoning. The larger model appear to be more conditioned to reason and will often fall into reasoning patterns even outside of the `<think>` `</think>` tags. That's what those repetitive failures always look like, e.g.:

```py
    # Parse the fractions
    x_num, x_den = x.split('/')
    n_num, n_den = n.split('/')

    # Multiply the fractions
    # (x_num / x_den) * (n_num / n_den) = (x_num * n_num) / (x_den * n_den)
    # Check if the result is a whole number
    # To do this, we can check if the numerator is divisible by the denominator
    # (x_num * n_num) % (x_den * n_den) == 0

    # But since we are working with integers, we can also check if the result is a whole number
    # by checking if the numerator is divisible by the denominator
    # (x_num * n_num) % (x_den * n_den) == 0
```

This is the type of stuff the model usually generates in its reasoning step, and it seems to work a lot better there, without needing repetition penalties to avoid falling into cycles. It seems like the non-reasoning mode is just sort of half-baked. The smaller Qwen3 models do a lot better with this style of prompting, to support that hypothesis. Qwen3-4B gets 78%, for instance. I think to actually get decent scores from Qwen3 in general the pipeline would have to allow for reasoning at the start of the prompt (i.e. generate until `</think>`, then inject the head of the function after that.

Repetition penalties in general are a hack, and you can't rely on them to fix a model that's already in some failure mode. In this case I think it's a bug in the implementation, though. Something about the combination of the forced prefix and the penalties being enabled causes it to always sample `!!!!!!!` before doing anything else, e.g.:

```py
def remove_vowels(text):
    """
    remove_vowels is a function that takes string and returns string without vowels.
    >>> remove_vowels('')
    ''
    >>> remove_vowels("abcdef\nghijklm")
    'bcdf\nghjklm'
    >>> remove_vowels('abcdef')
    'bcdf'
```

You should be able to test with repetition penalties now in the dev branch. Won't fix the thinking-in-comments exploit that Reka-Flash seems to have discovered, but it might help Qwen3-8B get back on track in a few cases where it gets stuck in a loop.

At the end of the day instruct models (and especially reasoning models) are just going to be harder to evaluate this way. HumanEval is also an old test by now and the problems presumably appear in all the pretraining datasets already. So the absolute score doesn't mean anything anymore. I mostly added it as an easy way to compare different quant levels of the same model against one another, and even that doesn't really seem to work anymore when more precise quants can get significantly *lower* scores, somehow.

Here are some results I just did with Qwen3-30B-A3B. Mostly within the margin of error for a single completion per task, but it's remarkable that a model with (presumably) the same training and finetuning data as Qwen3-8B is so much stronger on this particular test, and so much more consistently so:

| Model    | HumanEval pass@1 |
|----------|------------------|
| 2.25 bpw | 88.41%           |
| 3.00 bpw | 89.63%           |
| 4.00 bpw | 92.07%           |
| 5.00 bpw | 93.29%           |
| 6.00 bpw | 92.68%           |
| FP16     | 91.46%           |

And as mentioned, Qwen3-4B also performs much better. It's got to be worth looking into more rigorously. I'd imagine adding a little bit of random noise to the unquantized model could give you a similar effect in a more controlled way.

@turboderp with config/tokenizer_config/added_tokens from [here](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3-8B/tree/main) and your quant

| Model              | Q4   | Q6   | Q8   | FP16 |
| ------------------ | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| Qwen3-8B-exl3-4bpw | 86.0 | 85.4 | 86.0 | 87.2 |

Oohh. The only significant difference I can see is that those files don't define a `bos_token_id` in config.json.

So that makes sense. We've been fighting with this in TabbyAPI for a bit actually, that specifically Qwen3 (but only some versions of it) degrade significantly when there's a BOS token in the context. Don't know why that didn't occur to me here. It's been a real nightmare to try to work out exactly what the default is supposed to be for any given model, and what takes priority when there is conflicting information in the config. It looks like the Unsloth people solved it by just removing it from the config altogether.

I've reworked the prompt formatting a bit in the latest commit on the dev branch, so BOS isn't added by default except for those templates that should have it. And now it seems I'm also getting consistently good results from Qwen3-8B.

objects.body: The original [tokenizer_config.json](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/blob/main/tokenizer_config.json) also has `"add_bos_token": false` and `"bos_token": null` (same as all Qwen3 models), so maybe that should override `bos_token_id` from config.json.

@turboderp something else that is strange, on [Qwen3-0.6B](https://huggingface.co/turboderp/Qwen3-0.6B-exl3), `4.0bpw` and `8.0bpw_H8` branches, I'm getting 0% with `-cq 4` and `-cq 5`, but ~40% with `-cq 6`, same for 1.7B, 0% and ~70%, while 4B and up is always ~80% and up

The tokenizer function takes an explicit `add_bos` argument, and that shouldn't be interpreted as "maybe add a BOS token, unless the model's chat template says not to." The tokenizer in general doesn't care about templates, and that function has many other uses besides formatting an entire context for an instruct-tuned model. Arguably the problem with Qwen3 was that it defined a BOS token in the first place when clearly it's not meant to have one. Though it looks like maybe it goes a bit deeper than that, with *some* versions of Qwen3 being pretrained with BOS and some without? Idk.

In any case, the humaneval.py script should be more in line with the ever-evolving non-standard set by HF models :shrug:. It would maybe be more correct to use Transformers to extract the Jinja template from the model itself and always apply that, though there are potential complications with that approach as well.

As for cache quantizations, some models just don't work well if you compress the cache too much. Qwen3-0.6B isn't just a smaller version of Qwen3-4B, it's pretrained from scratch with different parameters, giving a different distribution of outliers in keys/values. It's not strange that it ends up being more sensitive to cache quantization if it tries to pack more information into its attn heads to begin with. You can try experimenting with values like `-cq 6,4` which has the same overall size as `-cq 5` but assigns more bits to the K channel.
